title: Early Polynesian Voyaging
titleline: Early Polynesian Voyaging - The History Web
para1: Early Polynesian Voyaging. Early Polynesian voyaging carried the descendants of the Lapita - Austronesian-speaking seafarers whose ancestral homeland was Taiwan - from western Polynesia out across the largest body of water on Earth. Having reached Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa by around 1000 BCE, Polynesian navigators went on to settle the far corners of the Polynesian triangle - Hawaii, Easter Island, and Aotearoa, an expanse encompassing more than 1,000 islands. This era matters profoundly because these seafarers developed the oceanic technologies and survival strategies that enabled humanity to inhabit the Pacific, deliberately migrating with crops like taro and yam and domestic animals to found permanent new colonies across the open ocean.
para2: Navigators crossed thousands of miles in outriggers and double canoes - like the ndrua of Fiji, with its unequal hulls - guided by a highly developed system of star paths, memorized sky charts, ocean swells, winds, and currents; knowledge so precious it was a closely guarded secret within navigator families, taught from an early age in places like the maneaba of Kiribati. Traditions like the legend of Kupe, who set off from Hawaiiki around 1300 CE to discover Aotearoa, encoded real navigational information - references to stars, wind patterns, and currents. Modern voyagers have proved the methods work: in 1965 a catamaran sailed from Tahiti to Aotearoa using no modern instruments, and in 1985 the 22-metre twin-hulled waka Hawaikinui recreated the old craft - a living refutation of doubters from Thor Heyerdahl's 1947 Kon-Tiki expedition onward. And the sweet potato, which entered Polynesian horticulture around 1000 CE, stands as strong evidence that these voyagers even reached the shores of South America and returned across the open Pacific.

title: Indigenous Australia (First Nations)
titleline: Indigenous Australia (First Nations) - The History Web
para1: Ancient Indigenous Australia (First Nations). Indigenous Australian societies represent one of the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth: archaeological evidence shows Aboriginal peoples have been living on this land for at least 65,000 years, confirming what Aboriginal people have always known. Their spiritual world is anchored in the Dreaming - the system of belief in which all-powerful beings roamed the landscape, laid down the moral and physical groundwork of the world, and gave life to the first people and their culture; no one can say exactly how old the Dreaming is, and from an Indigenous perspective it has existed from the beginning. At Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the discovery of Mungo Lady - the oldest known cremation in the world - and, just 300 metres away, of Mungo Man, both dated in 2003 to 40,000 years old, revolutionized understanding of the antiquity of these cultures: they are some of the oldest remains of modern humans ever discovered outside Africa.
para2: Far from living as simple wanderers, First Nations communities were custodians of Country, passing down ancient wisdom of its natural, human, and spiritual worlds. In the Kimberley, they carefully created a patchwork of firebreaks that slowed the spread of catastrophic wildfire sparked by lightning - traditional fire management that ecologists now combine with modern technology on a larger scale to reduce wildfire risk. Stone houses dating back 9,000 years, the oldest known in Australia, alongside shell middens and grinding stones, and boomerangs at least as old testify to settled skill, while a Pilbara cave holds evidence of Aboriginal life in northern Western Australia 50,000 years ago. Their languages, creation stories, and oral traditions preserved environmental memory and social law across dozens of millennia - a living heritage that First Nations people carry today.

title: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site
titleline: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site - The History Web
para1: The Kuk Early Agricultural Site. The Kuk Early Agricultural Site, located in the Western Highlands of Papua New Guinea, is a UNESCO World Heritage site where evidence suggests the land has been cultivated for at least 7,000 years - and perhaps, in its earliest phases, for nearly 10,000. Emerging around the same era as early farming in the Fertile Crescent and East Asia, Kuk matters because it is one of the few places in the world where archaeological evidence suggests an independent invention of agriculture: proof that Indigenous Papuan societies developed farming on their own, in total isolation from the other cradles of agriculture across the sea, in what may be one of the oldest continuously farmed landscapes anywhere on Earth - the site was inscribed on the World Heritage List in recognition of that outstanding testimony to a farming tradition born independently in the Pacific - a place where the deep history of agriculture can still be read directly from the soil.
para2: Excavations at Kuk reveal a well-preserved record of the great technical transformation from planting on mounds to draining the wetlands through ditches dug with wooden tools. The decisive shift came around 7,000-6,400 years ago, with organized farming based on the vegetative propagation of bananas, taro, and probably yams, and the site is an exceptional example of how agricultural practices changed across the ages. This horticultural tradition sustained dense highland populations for thousands of years; even today, modern farming at Kuk remains relatively low-key and does not intrude upon the archaeological features - ancient ditches and channels still legible beneath the working fields of the highland valley, where the same wetland that fed Papuan farmers for millennia now feeds their descendants and preserves their past.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: First Agricultural Revolution

title: The Lapita Culture
titleline: The Lapita Culture - The History Web
para1: The Lapita Culture. The Lapita culture was a prehistoric Pacific cultural complex dating between roughly 1600 and 500 BCE - presumably the culture of the original human settlers of Melanesia, much of Polynesia, and parts of Micronesia. Highly mobile seaborne explorers and colonists, they had established themselves on the Bismarck Archipelago northeast of New Guinea by 2000 BCE; beginning about 1600 BCE they spread to the Solomon Islands, and they had reached Fiji, Tonga, and the rest of western Polynesia by 1000 BCE, becoming the ancestors of the Polynesians, including the Maori - though archaeologists speak of a Lapita Cultural Complex, since the Lapita were not a homogeneous group. They matter because they carried farming, domesticated animals, and their distinctive stamped pottery across vast expanses of the Pacific, laying the foundation of the island world of Oceania.
para2: The Lapita are known principally from the remains of their fired pottery - beakers, cooking pots, and bowls - decorated with intricate geometric patterns made with a toothlike implement, with a few figurative designs; found from New Guinea eastward to Samoa, this pottery is the primary archaeological trail for tracking their migration. Their sites also yield fishhooks, pieces of obsidian and chert, and beads and rings made of shell. Skilled seafarers, they voyaged in double canoes or outriggers using nothing more than their knowledge of the stars and observations of the ocean, probably migrating deliberately, and able to survive for months on remote islands living on wild resources. They carried taro and yam and domestic animals with them - and the sweet potato that entered Polynesian horticulture around 1000 CE is strong evidence that their descendants made contact with South America.

title: The Austronesian Expansion
titleline: The Austronesian Expansion - The History Web
para1: The Austronesian Expansion. The Austronesian expansion (c. 3000-1000 BC) was the greatest seaborne migration of the prehistoric world, the movement of peoples who carried the Austronesian languages from Taiwan across half the globe. Beginning around 3000 BC, farming peoples crossed from the Asian mainland to Taiwan, where the Austronesian language family has its deepest roots. Over the following two thousand years their descendants moved south through the Philippines and into the islands of Southeast Asia, reaching Borneo, Java, and the coasts of New Guinea.
para2: The migrants were master seafarers. Sailing outrigger canoes across open ocean, they carried with them a whole way of life: domesticated pigs, dogs, and chickens, crops such as taro, yams, and bananas, pottery, and stone tools. By about 1500 BC one branch of these voyagers had reached the Bismarck Archipelago east of New Guinea, where archaeologists recognize them as the makers of Lapita pottery, vessels decorated with intricate stamped designs that have been found across thousands of kilometers of the southwest Pacific.
para3: From the Bismarcks the Lapita people pushed onward into the unknown. In a few centuries they had settled island groups across a vast arc, from New Caledonia and Vanuatu to Fiji, Tonga, and Samoa, voyaging farther into remote Oceania than any people before them. Much later their descendants would make the final astonishing leaps, reaching Hawaii, Easter Island, and New Zealand, and westward across the Indian Ocean to Madagascar.
para4: The expansion left a single linguistic and cultural inheritance across an oceanic world: today the Austronesian languages, from Malagasy in Madagascar to Hawaiian and Maori in the Pacific, are spoken by some four hundred million people. The Lapita colonization of the Pacific stands as one of humanity's supreme achievements of exploration, accomplished with stone tools, woven sails, and an unmatched knowledge of the sea.

title: The First Settlement of Fiji and Samoa
titleline: The First Settlement of Fiji and Samoa - The History Web
para1: The First Settlement of Fiji and Samoa. The first settlement of Fiji and Samoa, beginning around 1300 BC, carried humanity across the last great water barrier of the southwest Pacific. The settlers were the Lapita people, seafarers from the islands southeast of New Guinea, whose distinctive pottery marks their trail. At sites such as Bourewa and Natunuku on the Fijian island of Viti Levu, archaeologists have found the remains of their beachside villages: decorated pottery, shell ornaments, obsidian traded over hundreds of kilometers of sea, and the bones of the animals they carried with them.
para2: These first Fijians and Samoans were skilled farmers, fishers, and sailors. They planted taro and yams in gardens cleared from the coastal forest, fished the reefs with hooks of shell, and kept pigs and chickens, while maintaining ties with the islands they had come from. In Samoa, Lapita settlements such as the Mulifanua site on Upolu mark the western edge of the same great dispersal, which reached Tonga at about the same time as Fiji.
para3: Over the following centuries the settler societies grew and changed. Pottery styles evolved and then faded away, populations expanded inland and into the hills, and long-distance exchange networks slowly contracted as the islands became self-sufficient. Out of these Lapita communities emerged the ancestors of the Fijian, Tongan, and Samoan peoples, and the foundations of the chiefly societies that later Europeans would encounter.
para4: The settlement of Fiji and Samoa was a turning point in Pacific history. It completed the colonization of the island groups within reach of inter-island voyaging, and it paused on the edge of an even greater ocean: after a long standstill of perhaps two thousand years, the descendants of these first settlers would sail on to discover and settle the remote islands of Polynesia, from the Marquesas to Hawaii, Easter Island, and New Zealand.
